comments.author: BenjaminRi
comments.text: I don't feel the same way. To the contrary: AI takes lots of little problems off my shoulders, which means I must think even harder because more of the tougher, bigger problems come my way. This feels very similar to when you are moved into a leadership position and need to assess the work packages and delegate them. All the tough issues that the juniors face come back to you if your instructions were unclear. So it's up to you to work out exactly what should be done, and how, and only greenlight implementations that do the right thing.

comments.author: etler
comments.text: I feel the same way, in fact, AI has enabled me to think even harder because I didn't use it to think for me, I use it to teach me. The world of CS is massive and any one of us only know our little corner of that world. AI research gives me a wider view into that world that's too big for me to explore without a guide. I'm exploring concepts I never would have find without LLMs acting as a great domain space search tool. I'm not thinking less, if anything I have too much to think about.

comments.text:

comments.author: BenjaminRi
comments.text:
When I've worked in a leadership position, I was rarely thinking very hard about the work. If you were, consider that you may have been micromanaging.


It really depends on who is working for you. There are some people, even straight from uni, who you can just roughly tell to do such-and-such and they'll go ahead and do it and solve all the problems on their own, using their own judgement if they get stuck or face ambiguity. Then there are people who return to you and ask for advice every time they face an obstacle. AI is obviously more of the latter right now.

Ultimately, what matters to me is the result, including the quality of the written code and the architectural design choices taken. If I delegate those and it turns out great, I have no complaints.

comments.author: inactive-user
comments.text:
Also came to write a similar comment. For me, LLMs aren't code output mulitpliers but thinking accelerators.

Being able to deeply dive into a topic and having something next to you that asynchronously can validate or reject your ideas quickly is a surprisingly strong booster for thinking.

My main use for LLMs is definitly reviewing  ideas, designs and APIs. I figured that sometimes, it just boosts your own creativity and insight into a problem if you're giving the LLM the task to primarily question your decisions and make you  justify every decision you make.

One of my base prompt shapes is this:


I have this rough idea:

<insert idea here>

Ask me 20 questions, and after each question await my answer. then summarize the discussion and give me a short list of open topics to be solved.


This style of brainstorming is really effective for me, and made me much more of a "Thinker" than i was before.

I started to like thinking through topics deeply since i've become a dad, as my hobby coding/dev time has grown very little, and having basically solved a problem when you boot your PC makes you a really effective developer.

comments.author: BinaryIgor
comments.text:
Exactly; with LLMs, I would agree that the default way of using them can make you lazy and think less and milder.

But, if you are driven and intentional, you might arguably think broader, deeper, harder and more than you could have in any other period of the human history.

Fascinating times to be alive for serious thinkers!

comments.author: nrdxp
comments.text: Indeed, I'd say "thinking" is one major area you should never expect the LLM to outdo you in. Perhaps if it feels this way, you just need to up the stakes a bit?

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text: «Never» is a strong word; symbolic AIs had moments of outthinking people even in 1990s, and I see where some kinds of outthinking can come from LLMs today. (And this includes open mathematical/TCS problems). Not all thinking is better fitting humans than machines…

comments.author: nrdxp
comments.text: Yeah, sure, I suppose I'm mostly refering to novel problem solving, which is consistently among the lowest scores in common benchmarks for these machines. Hence the "up the stakes" take. In other words, you might just need to find problems with little to no prior art to challenge the old noodle a bit.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
I'm referring to inventing proofs for open problems in mathematics (theoretical CS included), which is at least hard to separate from novel problem solving. I expect symbolic AIs to optimise well a search for a novel small construction in the heart of the proof — sometimes resolving what humans did not; and I expect LLM AIs to (with proper harness, eventually, sometimes) figure out that a completely unexpected thing can be retargeted as prior art for an open question.

Of course, like different human styles fit better different problems, AI styles fit well specific kinds of problems. But raising the stakes is not enough, you have to be ready to retreat from some topics into the topics where you are not at disadvantage.

comments.author: zladuric
comments.text:
I see where this is coming from.
There are some concepts and ideas in the article that I certainly agree with.

But to me, a lot of stuff at work had left the realm of thinking a long time ago. We used to have lots of problems to think about, when writing software. Then over the decades, we solved them most.

We also scaled the field so much that there are so many software engineers, developers and hackers that there's not enough problems we can all be working on all in parallel. Or at least, not enough VCs willing to finance all of those things. So they pick a few problems and brute force the solutions.

You still have hard problem here and there, but I feel like the most of us are just implementing known solutions to known problems. Oh, the AI copilot schemes are new, prompt optimisation and operations are actively worked on.

Fields like medicine or finance or whatever industry have new tools to work with so we are thinking hard how to solve them.

But I think only a tiny majority of people building software have the possibility to rely think about the problems they're solving. Most of us are just in it to produce more of this or that.

It's probably a lot of people, but it's a tiny fragment of all of us in the field. Don't get me wrong, I'd love to work on such problems where you can't sleep because it's bugging you, but I know the chance of landing something like that is rare. I mostly just work for the money now.

comments.author: rbr
comments.text:
I miss having an easy backup for when my career in academia crashes :(

Alas. To contribute to the discussion, in even the smallest a way:


"If you can ‘vibe code’ your way through it, the problem wasn’t actually hard."


In this vein, I figured that if students have access to LLMs for projects and reports, we should just raise the bar above what an LLM can achieve. However, in courses being given around me, the prevailing approach seems to be to provide grading opportunities where LLMs are excluded (oral exams, pen-and-paper exams). Combined with urging the student to actually engage with the material, and not to let the LLM do it. It seems to be kind of working.

In hindsight, my idea seems shortsighted: raising the bar like that would start requiring most students to use LLMs, which should be avoided at all costs. Let's not push the (unexplored) ethical and moral burdens of LLM usage onto students for as long as we can.

comments.author: albertorestifo
comments.text:
I share my feelings with the Author.

If I'm debugging a production issue, I could spend time thinking hard, carefully combing trough the flow and analyze the situation, or I can dump the production logs to a LLM and ask what is wrong, getting correct theory back virtually instantly, no thinking required.

comments.author: henderson
comments.text:
I think this is a big part of the reason that I miss university. But I don't know how much thinking I get to do at work, and how much of it is hard thinking vs just trying to juggle the various responsibilities I have.

What made difficult problems fun/interesting at university was in part the social dynamic. It was fun and enriching to work on difficult problems in class, to talk them over with my classmates, etc.

And you can formulate a similar environment outside of university - I teach a community college course and that's a great place to think hard. Or a book club, a local programming group. There's https://paperswelove.org/ in lots of places and starting a local chapter would be an enriching thing maybe too, if there isn't one already.
